Yes—recent papers suggest linear-time long-context recall can be improved, but different methods target different bottlenecks. Raven directly targets recall in linear-time sequence models by reducing interference from dense state updates and avoiding hard eviction, reporting strong long-context recall where sliding-window attention and state-space models degrade, including at much longer contexts than seen in training [1]. Kaczmarz Linear Attention improves state updates in delta-rule recurrent models and reports strong retrieval and associative recall results while remaining stable at long contexts [2]. Adaptive Memory Decay for log-linear attention also improves long-range memory by making decay input-dependent while preserving its log-linear complexity [3].

The papers also explain why recall is hard: fixed-size recurrent memory causes shared storage, interference, and capacity limits, with memory load hurting recall more than elapsed context in the tested regime [5]. A related ARMT approach extends LLM context with associative recurrent memory, reporting processing beyond original context limits and better generalization to out-of-distribution context lengths with lower FLOPs [9].
